doc.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: The bassist's role: time, feeling and being a team player
summary: Moore describes how he teaches bass: time and feel first, the catcher analogy, and keeping volume in balance with the piano.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: If you were talking to a group of young musicians, which I know you do a lot, can you describe how you think of your role as a bassist?

Sure. Well I do a lot of teaching and I think that the bass is probably — maybe as Dizzy said that’s the first thing he’d get for a big band was a good bass player, and he’d go from there. And I think it is probably that — I wouldn’t say the most important — but right in there with the drums and the piano and the rhythm, it’s very central. And the feel, the team spirit that you have to develop as a bass player I think is very important. I don’t care about the solos, that can come later. But I always tell bass players, time, feeling, is the most important thing that you have to shoot for right away, and work towards that. And solos later on, or at the same time, but never, never forgetting the function of the instrument. And you really have to, in a way, a lot of times a great bass player I think is not noticed. I correlate it to being a catcher. I used to be a catcher in baseball. And I think about it as kind of the catcher. He’s not noticed on a ball field, until he makes a mistake. And the bass player is kind of the same way. You shouldn’t be noticed that much. You should be felt, and the rhythm should sound good, but the bass shouldn’t — until it comes to the solo — he shouldn’t stand out as like playing a lot of tricks and things like this. There have been a lot of bass players through the last century that stand out no matter what they do. But I think when you’re accompanying you should not disappear, but you should not be so noticeable until it comes time to play solos. And that takes a certain amount of almost Zen attitude of thinking about the unit and putting yourself out in front of the audience and saying how is the band sounding, and thinking about the rhythm section as a unit. And volume has a lot to do with it. You can’t be too loud because then you overpower the acoustic instruments on the bandstand. It’s very important to set your volume, if you’re using an amplifier, to the keyboards, the piano in particular, the acoustic piano. Because it can’t get any louder than that is. So if you crank up the amplifier, then the whole thing is destroyed. You haven’t got a chance. So there’s a lot of
elements that go into it, but mainly being a team player, and kind of maybe subjugating your ego just a little bit, to do it.
